task_title: Technology in the Cockpit: EFBs, PEDs and Unfamiliar Aircraft
area: Area VI. Safety and Risk Management
objective: By the end of this lesson you can use an electronic flight bag and other portable devices within the rules and their limits, manage automation without losing situational awareness, and plan a safe transition to a new aircraft or avionics system.
why: Tablets, glass panels and autopilots are now in most cockpits, and the FAA says over-reliance on automation has caused accidents. A 2010 NTSB study cited in AC 61-98E found glass cockpit airplanes had a lower total accident rate but a higher fatal accident rate than the same types with analog instruments [[15:13|AC 61-98E 2.2.2]]. AC 90-109A adds that the main factor in fatal airplane accidents is pilot performance, especially when moving to an unfamiliar airplane [[57:2|AC 90-109A 3d]].

prereading.what: What an EFB is, the four criteria for replacing paper, portable versus installed EFBs, and what to assess and train.
prereading.label: AC 91-78A pp 2 to 4

prereading.what: The portable electronic device rule and who decides which devices may be used.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.21

prereading.what: Why 91.21 exists, how an operator decides a device will not interfere, and what to do if it does.
prereading.label: AC 91.21-1D pp 1 to 5

prereading.what: Automation levels, anticipate, act and verify, and the flight mode annunciator.
prereading.label: RMH 7-1 to 7-4

prereading.what: Managing information, automation and risk in an advanced avionics airplane.
prereading.label: PHAK 2-29 to 2-32

prereading.what: How to study a new airplane: systems, procedures, performance and limitations.
prereading.label: AC 90-109A pp 13 to 18

prereading.what: Manual flight after automation failure, automation bias and how instructors should test it.
prereading.label: AC 61-98E 2-4 to 2-6

warmup: Think first: you just bought a share in a fixed-gear, 310 hp single with a glass panel and a two-axis autopilot. Today you fly a steam-gauge trainer and plan every flight on a tablet. Before you take your family on an IFR trip in the new airplane, what would you study, who would you fly with, and what would you do if the tablet went dark and the autopilot dropped a mode in the clouds?

key_terms.def: An electronic display system used mainly in the flight deck or cabin. It can show paper information such as checklists, charts and the POH, and do calculations such as weight and balance and performance.
An EFB that does not need aircraft power or navigation input to display, is not attached to an aircraft mounting device, and is not connected to any aircraft system.
An EFB that may take protected aircraft power, take position from an onboard navigation system, and sit in an approved mount.
A carried-on consumer device such as a phone, tablet or laptop. Your EFB tablet is one.
A PED that radiates on purpose, such as a mobile phone or a computer with wireless networking.
In 14 CFR, an airplane with an electronically advanced avionics system: an electronic PFD, an MFD with a GPS moving map, and a two axis autopilot tied to navigation and heading guidance.
The strip on the PFD that shows which autopilot modes are engaged and which are armed.
The RMH steps for any automation input: know what should happen, make the input, then check that it happened.
Trusting the automation because you feel it is more capable than you. It leads to passive "set and go" flying.
Overconfidence from repeated experience. Highly reliable automation tends to cause it.
An airplane with an engine of more than 200 horsepower. 61.31(f) requires training and a one-time endorsement to act as PIC.
An airplane with retractable landing gear, flaps and a controllable pitch propeller (or a FADEC engine control). 61.31(e) requires training and a one-time endorsement.

chunks.title: EFBs: what AC 91-78A lets them replace

body.p: AC 91-78A is the Part 91 guide for replacing required paper information with an EFB and for using EFB databases and apps [[42:1|AC 91-78A 1]]. It is not mandatory and is not a regulation. It describes an acceptable means, not the only means, but if you use its means you must follow it in all important respects [[42:1|AC 91-78A 1]].

An EFB is an electronic display system used mainly in the flight deck or cabin. It can show paper information such as checklists, charts and the POH, and can do calculations such as weight and balance, performance and fuel [[42:2|AC 91-78A 7.1]]. EFBs can store and retrieve the POH and supplements, MELs, charts and terminal procedures [[42:2|AC 91-78A 8]].

head: AC 91-78A 9.1: an EFB may replace paper in all phases of flight when...
What it means for you
rows: It does not replace any system or equipment required by Part 91, such as a navigation, communication or surveillance system [[42:3|AC 91-78A 9.1]]
The tablet is never your required radio or transponder.
It shows only information functionally equivalent to the paper it replaces [[42:3|AC 91-78A 9.1]]
The electronic POH or chart must say what the paper one says.
Information used for navigation or performance planning is current, up to date and valid, as verified by the pilot [[42:3|AC 91-78A 9.1]]
You check the data cycle, not the app.
The operator complies with 91.21 so the EFB does not interfere with required equipment [[42:3|AC 91-78A 9.1]]
Your EFB is a PED, so 91.21 applies to it.

callout.text: In-flight use of an EFB in place of paper is the decision of the aircraft operator and the PIC. Any Type A or Type B EFB application (as AC 120-76 defines them) may be substituted for the paper equivalent with no formal operational approval, as long as the AC is followed [[42:3|AC 91-78A 9.2]].

bullets: AC 91-78A lists the related rules: 91.21 (PEDs), 91.103 (preflight action), 91.503 and 91.1033 [[42:1|AC 91-78A 5]].

91.9(b) requires a current, approved flight manual (or, where one is not required, approved manual material, markings and placards) to be available in the aircraft [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9]]. Interpretation: if your copy lives on the tablet, the 9.1 tests above are how you show it meets the paper standard, and the tablet has to be on board and working.
Pilots stay responsible for proper use of an EFB or installed avionics, and may be evaluated on it during a practical test [[1:334|PHAK 13-24]].

callout.text: Changed: AC 91-78A (dated 2/23/24) cancels AC 91-78, Use of Class 1 or Class 2 EFB, dated July 20, 2007 [[42:1|AC 91-78A 4]]. The new AC sorts EFBs as portable or installed instead of by class [[42:3|AC 91-78A 10.1]] [[42:3|AC 91-78A 10.2]].

check.q: Your EFB shows an approach chart from a cycle that has expired. Which AC 91-78A criterion does that break?
check.a: 9.1(3): information used for navigation or performance planning must be current, up to date and valid, as verified by the pilot [[42:3|AC 91-78A 9.1]].

chunks.title: Portable or installed, and fitting it into your cockpit

head: Portable EFB
Installed EFB
rows: Not dependent on a dedicated aircraft power source or navigation input to display. May plug into aircraft power through a certificated power source [[42:3|AC 91-78A 10.1]]
May take aircraft power from a bus protected by a properly rated breaker or fuse [[42:3|AC 91-78A 10.2]]
Not attached to an aircraft mounting device [[42:3|AC 91-78A 10.1]]
May sit in a mounting device approved for installation; for a type-certificated aircraft the mount must meet 21.303 [[42:3|AC 91-78A 10.2]]
Not connected with or receiving data from any aircraft system [[42:3|AC 91-78A 10.1]]
May take position from an onboard navigation system if designed so it does not upset that system's output [[42:3|AC 91-78A 10.2]]. AC 20-173 covers installation [[42:4|AC 91-78A 10.2]]

body.p: A hand-held unit needs no approval, but modifying the aircraft for it, such as an external antenna or a permanent mounting bracket, does [[33:101|AIM TBL 1-1-6]]. A panel or yoke mounted holder is governed by 14 CFR part 43, so ask your mechanic [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17b1(c)(3)]].

bullets: AC 91-78A asks the operator to assess workload, how the EFB fits into the flight deck, display and lighting, system shutdown and system failures [[42:4|AC 91-78A 11.1]].
It also asks about stowage for takeoff and landing and an unsecured EFB, and warns that using the controls can be harder in flight [[42:4|AC 91-78A 11.1]].

Training should cover preflight checks of the system, each function you use, any phases of flight when the EFB should not be used, and how to cross-check data entry and computed results [[42:4|AC 91-78A 11.2]].
At night, set the EFB brightness so it does not seriously impair night vision [[24:222|AFH 11-5]].

callout.text: Load the plan on the ground. The AIM says VFR waypoints for a flight should be loaded on the ground, and pilots should avoid programming routes once airborne [[33:91|AIM 1-1-17b1(e)(5)]]. The same habit cuts head-down time with any EFB.

check.q: Name the three things that make an EFB "portable" under AC 91-78A.
check.a: It does not depend on a dedicated aircraft power source or navigation input to display, it is not attached to an aircraft mounting device, and it is not connected to or receiving data from any aircraft system [[42:3|AC 91-78A 10.1]].

chunks.title: Keeping the EFB working, current and honest

body.p: Be familiar with the device's operation, capabilities and limitations before you use it. Like paper, the database has to be current; databases are updated every 28 days [[23:30|IFH 1-11]]. Most of the limits below are in the AIM's VFR GPS guidance, and they apply to any tablet moving map.

head: Limit
What to do
rows: Database currency. Required for IFR, recommended for all other use, not required for VFR [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17b1(c)(2)]]

Do not use an outdated moving map around critical airspace; check waypoints against current charts or the Chart Supplement [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17b1(c)(2)]]. Without a current database, disregard the map for critical navigation decisions [[1:419|PHAK 16-32]]
No RAIM. VFR panel units and hand-held units cannot alert you to too few satellites or a position error [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17b1(c)(1)]]
Cross-check with other navigation and be suspicious of the GPS if the two disagree [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17b1(c)(1)]]
Antenna. Suction-cup antennas inside the windows lose signals; with no RAIM, the position can be wrong with no warning [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17b1(c)(3)]]
Treat the tablet's position as an aid, not the truth
Jamming and spoofing can put a wrong aircraft position on the moving map and EFB [[33:119|AIM 1-2-4c]]
Tell ATC about GPS degradation and be ready to navigate without GPS [[33:118|AIM 1-2-4a]]
Data link weather is old. Assume it is at least 7 to 8 minutes older than its time stamp [[1:334|PHAK 13-24]]
Use it only for broad strategic avoidance [[1:334|PHAK 13-24]] [[28:25|AWH 3-2]]
Too much information. Layered products add to workload [[1:334|PHAK 13-24]]
Show only what this phase of flight needs [[1:334|PHAK 13-24]]

callout.text: Watch out: no design standard of accuracy or integrity is used for a VFR GPS receiver, so do not rely on it alone [[33:91|AIM 1-1-17b1(d)]]. VFR and hand-held GPS units are not authorized for IFR navigation, instrument approaches or as a primary instrument flight reference. Under IFR they are only an aid to situational awareness [[33:101|AIM TBL 1-1-6]].

body.p: Power and failure: AC 91-78A asks you to assess system shutdown and system failures [[42:4|AC 91-78A 11.1]], but the sources give no battery, heat or backup-device rule. Application: before each flight, decide how you will finish it if the screen goes dark (installed avionics, a second device or paper) and keep that backup reachable.

check.q: Your VFR tablet map has an expired database and shows you clear of a restricted area. What do the AIM and PHAK say?
check.a: Check the airspace and waypoints against current products such as the sectional or Chart Supplement [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17b1(c)(2)]], and disregard the outdated map for critical navigation decisions [[1:419|PHAK 16-32]].

chunks.title: PEDs and 91.21: your own devices count

body.p: RF.IV.D covered passengers' devices and the briefing. This chunk is about the devices you fly with. The rule exists because of interference: it began in May 1961 as a ban on FM receivers that disturbed aircraft navigation and communication systems [[43:1|AC 91.21-1D 6.1]] [[43:2|AC 91.21-1D 6.1]].

callout.text: 91.21(a): no person may operate, and no operator or PIC may allow, any PED on a U.S.-registered civil aircraft operated by an air carrier or operating certificate holder, or on any other aircraft while it is operated under IFR. (b) excepts voice recorders, hearing aids, pacemakers, electric shavers and any PED the operator has determined will not interfere with the navigation or communication system. (c) for aircraft other than certificate holders', the PIC or other operator may make that determination [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21]].

bullets: Your tablet is a PED. Any PED use must be evaluated by the user or operator before use so it will not interfere in any way with the operation of the aircraft [[42:2|AC 91-78A 7.2]].
So on an IFR flight in your own or a rented airplane, using the tablet is your determination as PIC [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21]].

By regulation only the operator is responsible for permitting a PED technology. If you lack knowledge of the methods, consult a trained and knowledgeable expert [[43:4|AC 91.21-1D 7.1]]. AC 91.21-1D uses "operator" to mean the PIC, renter-pilot or certificate holder [[43:2|AC 91.21-1D 6.1]].

An aircraft designed and certified PED tolerant may allow use in all phases. An aircraft with an FAA-approved system such as installed Wi-Fi is PED tolerant for PEDs used with that system [[43:4|AC 91.21-1D 7.2.1]].
If the aircraft has not been shown PED tolerant, PED use may be allowed in cruise. If interference appears, isolate the device, record the conditions and turn it off [[43:5|AC 91.21-1D 7.2.3]].

callout.text: Note: paragraph 1 of AC 91.21-1D sums 91.21 up as an IFR rule [[43:1|AC 91.21-1D 1]]. The rule text also covers every aircraft operated by an air carrier or operating certificate holder, VFR included [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21]]. Teach the rule text.

check.q: On an IFR flight in a flying club airplane, who decides whether your tablet may be used?
check.a: The PIC or other operator of the aircraft [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21]], here you as PIC [[43:2|AC 91.21-1D 6.1]].

chunks.title: Interference: transmitters, Bluetooth, GPS and battery fires

body.p: Transmitting PEDs (T-PEDs) radiate on purpose: mobile phones, computers with wireless networking and similar devices [[43:3|AC 91.21-1D 6.8]]. Even non-transmitting PEDs give off spurious emissions, which is why the tolerance standard covers both kinds [[43:3|AC 91.21-1D 6.9]].

head: Source
What the sources say
rows: Cellular
The FCC prohibits airborne cellular phone operation (47 CFR 22.925). Phones off, cellular transmit off, or airplane mode while airborne [[43:7|AC 91.21-1D 9.1]] [[43:7|AC 91.21-1D 9.2]]
Bluetooth and other low-power links

In its section on cargo-tracking devices, AC 91.21-1D quotes RTCA DO-363: low-power emissions (limit 100 mW EIRP) do not affect aircraft systems, and Bluetooth is one of them. Wi-Fi (WLAN) devices often have far more output than 100 mW [[43:8|AC 91.21-1D 10.3.2]]
GPS
Unintentional interference can come from GPS repeaters and even some systems on board the aircraft [[33:118|AIM 1-2-4b]]
Batteries

Operator PED procedures should cover PED unit or battery smoke or fire [[43:5|AC 91.21-1D 8.1]]. In its unmanned aircraft chapter, the AIM lists lithium batteries as dangerous goods that temperature and pressure changes can make leak, give off fumes or catch fire [[34:249|AIM 11-4-5c]]

callout.text: If a radio, CDI or GPS acts up and you suspect a device: isolate it, note the conditions, and turn it off [[43:5|AC 91.21-1D 7.2.3]]. Application: switch devices off one at a time while you watch the symptom, and fly the airplane first. Operators are also expected to have a way to report PED interference to a responsible Flight Standards office [[43:6|AC 91.21-1D 8.2]].

body.p: Application: this is why the 9.1 criteria tie the EFB to 91.21 [[42:3|AC 91-78A 9.1]]. A tablet with a cellular radio, a Wi-Fi hotspot and a Bluetooth receiver is three transmitters next to your radios.

check.q: Which low-power standard does the DO-363 quote in AC 91.21-1D name, and which kind of device does the AC warn often exceeds that level?
check.a: Bluetooth (and ZigBee) at or below 100 mW EIRP; WLAN (Wi-Fi) devices often exceed it [[43:8|AC 91.21-1D 10.3.2]].

body.p: Automation takes a pilot input and aircraft information, works out a solution, and flies it without continuous input. Used properly it reduces workload, improves situational awareness and frees attention for the flight path [[30:50|RMH 7-1]].

bullets: You choose the level. Use automation to manage workload, not to make up for a lack of proficiency [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].
One of the most common errors is failing to move to a lower level of automation when the situation changes [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

Example: ATC cancels your approach clearance after the IAF and gives vectors to a hold. Select basic heading and altitude modes, then reprogram while the flight path stays under control [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].
If the automation is not doing what you expect, reduce the level, fly manually and take time to sort it out [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

body.p: For every button push or knob turn: Anticipate (know what should happen), Act (make the input), Verify (check the aircraft or avionics did it) [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

In RMH Figure 7-3 the green annunciators show the autopilot engaged in heading and altitude modes at 9,000 ft, and the white LOC and GS show approach mode armed but not engaged [[30:52|RMH 7-3]]. Know at all times which modes are engaged and which are armed, and verify armed functions engage when they should. Callouts help, even single pilot [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]].

callout.text: Watch out: with some autopilots, changing the e-HSI navigation source from GPS to LOC or VOR while in NAV mode drops NAV. Lateral control defaults to ROL (wings level) until you reengage NAV [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]. A pilot without training may not anticipate this [[30:52|RMH 7-3]].
Application, for displays colored like RMH Figure 7-3: "Green is flying, white is waiting." Colors differ by system, so learn your own from its pilot guide [[30:53|RMH 7-4]].

check.q: ATC cancels your approach clearance after the IAF and says expect to hold. What level of automation does the RMH suggest while you reprogram?
check.a: Basic autopilot modes that control heading and altitude, so the flight path stays under control while you program and configure [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

chunks.title: Risk: over-reliance, complacency and lost situational awareness

body.p: AC 61-98E says over-reliance on automation has caused accidents. It describes automation bias: trusting the automation because you feel it is more capable than you, which leads to passive "set and go" management and erodes manual skills [[15:13|AC 61-98E 2.2.2]]. The AIH adds that highly reliable automation breeds complacency, so a pilot may follow it against common sense and stop crosschecking [[25:18|AIH 1-14]].

bullets: Humans are poor monitors of automation. The more reliable the system, the poorer the human monitoring [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]].
A pilot who only follows the magenta line can fly into high terrain or prohibited airspace, or be lost when the map fails [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]] [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]].
AFMs prohibit using the moving map, terrain, traffic and weather data link displays as the primary data source [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]].
Concentrating on tablets reduces how often you scan for traffic, so limit that time [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g]].

An ADS-B traffic display is not a collision avoidance system and does not relieve you of see and avoid [[33:304|AIM 4-5-7e]]. TIS-B targets update about every 3 to 13 seconds, ADS-B about once a second [[33:306|AIM 4-5-8d2(c)]].
Pilots who always fly on the autopilot can lose the ability to fly manually when the system disconnects, for example in icing [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

callout.text: Watch out: in an FMS accident in Colombia, the airplane flew its programmed path into mountainous terrain [[30:52|RMH 7-3]]. The PHAK says a waypoint was entered incorrectly, and the crew had charts and a navigation log but let the automation manage itself [[1:71|PHAK 2-32]].

head: Defense
Source
rows: Keep track of aircraft position, flight path, other aircraft, the environment and human factors
Before departure, check all programming and compare the route with a paper log; if they differ, do not assume the computer is right
Use all navigation equipment, such as VOR to back up GPS and vice versa
Match the automation to your proficiency and stay within personal limits
Actively manage: cross-reference systems and monitor waypoints and checkpoints
Hand fly at times to keep manual skills

check.q: What did the 2010 NTSB study cited in AC 61-98E find about glass cockpit airplanes?
check.a: A lower total accident rate but a higher fatal accident rate than the same types with analog instruments [[15:13|AC 61-98E 2.2.2]].

chunks.title: Unfamiliar aircraft: what the rules require

body.p: Accidents from loss of control or situational awareness often come from a pilot not ready for what the new aircraft demands. A transitioning pilot needs training in its systems and characteristics, including normal, abnormal and emergency procedures [[57:1|AC 90-109A 3a]]. AC 90-109A is written mainly for experimental airplanes, but its recommendations also apply to unfamiliar type-certificated aircraft [[57:2|AC 90-109A 3d]].

head: To act as PIC of...
You need
Source
rows: A complex airplane (retractable gear, flaps, controllable pitch prop, or FADEC)
Logged ground and flight training, found proficient, one-time endorsement
A high-performance airplane (engine of more than 200 hp)
Logged ground and flight training, found proficient, one-time endorsement
A pressurized aircraft with a service ceiling or maximum operating altitude above 25,000 ft MSL
Ground training and flight training, with endorsements
An aircraft the FAA says needs type-specific training
Logged type-specific training and an endorsement
A tailwheel airplane
Logged flight training and an endorsement
A large aircraft or a turbojet
A type rating

body.p: Part 61 defines a TAA [[60:187|14 CFR 61.1(b)]] and lists its parts (electronic PFD, MFD with a GPS moving map, two axis autopilot) in 61.129(j) [[60:321|14 CFR 61.129(j)]], but 61.31 has no endorsement for glass panels or autopilots. AC 61-98E says pilots moving to a TAA should get specialized transition training from an instructor experienced with that equipment [[15:26|AC 61-98E 4.3.3]]. Interpretation: the endorsements are the legal floor, not a full transition.

callout.text: 91.103: before a flight the PIC must become familiar with all available information, including runway lengths and the AFM takeoff and landing distance data [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]]. AC 90-109A ties this to unfamiliar airplanes: without an approved flight manual, use other reliable information appropriate to the aircraft [[57:18|AC 90-109A 8d]].

Watch out: there is as much risk moving down in performance as moving up. High-speed, high-altitude experience does not prepare a pilot for a low-inertia, high-drag airplane [[57:3|AC 90-109A 5c]]. In a slower airplane, weather and headwinds (as a percentage) hit harder, crosswind ability may be lower and avionics may be less capable. Going from a multi-crew airplane to single pilot brings its own challenges [[57:52|AC 90-109A App 10]].

check.q: Your new airplane has fixed gear, flaps, a constant-speed prop and a 230 hp engine. Which 61.31 training and endorsement apply?
check.a: High-performance, because the engine has more than 200 hp [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(f)]]. It is not complex, since it has no retractable gear [[24:232|AFH 12-1]].

chunks.title: Learning a new airplane or avionics system

body.p: AC 90-109A says to study, as applicable: systems (fuel, electrical, hydraulic, flight controls, gear, environmental, avionics, powerplant, autoflight, flight instruments, warning, oxygen, emergency equipment), procedures (normal, abnormal, emergency), performance (takeoff and landing, climb, cruise, descent, glide) and limitations (weight, CG, V speeds, kinds of operation, crosswind, landing surface) [[57:14|AC 90-109A 8a]].

bullets: Use the flow method: follow fuel from the filler port to the cylinder, or current from the battery and alternator through the buses to each user [[57:15|AC 90-109A 8b]] [[57:16|AC 90-109A 8b]].
Learn what normal looks like, so you can spot abnormal; high oil pressure is normal after a cold start but not in cruise [[57:18|AC 90-109A 8c]].
Use a checklist in every airplane, however simple [[57:16|AC 90-109A 8c]]. An alternator failure may be an inconvenience in day VFR but an emergency at night or in IFR [[57:18|AC 90-109A 8c]].

Sit in the airplane on the ground until you can find every control without searching. In the "blindfold test" an assistant calls out controls and switches and you find them by memory [[57:44|AC 90-109A App 7]].

callout.text: Watch out: in an NTSB case, a new owner of an amateur-built airplane with a moved, unmarked fuel selector behind the left shoulder had a half-hour checkout. Reaching for the selector in flight, he pressed right rudder and lost control [[57:43|AC 90-109A App 7]]. Inadequate transition training and no experience in the type were factors [[57:44|AC 90-109A App 7]].

body.p: For avionics, learn the system at a conceptual level; knob-and-dial steps are not enough. Expect surprises, use simulation software and books, and "stop, look and read" before pushing buttons [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]]. Most GPS receivers are not intuitive, and some makers offer tutorials or simulators [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17b1(b)]]. Know the autopilot disconnect and emergency procedures and where the checklists are; read the system documentation and AFM supplements [[30:53|RMH 7-4]].

bullets: PHAK's two rules for electronic flight displays: be able to fly the aircraft to standard, and read and understand the installed systems' manuals, including the autopilot [[1:68|PHAK 2-29]].

Glass-panel preflight checks may include the flight deck reference guide on board, red X's clearing over engine indications, alarms and annunciators, and avionics cooling fans. The AFM/POH says how [[24:42|AFH 2-5]].
Not every EFIS has a reversionary mode or an MFD, so learn what your system has [[24:345|AFH 17-11]].
Unfamiliarity with the aircraft or its systems is a hazard with high risk potential, not something to accept casually [[1:66|PHAK 2-27]].

check.a: An assistant calls out controls and switches and the pilot locates each one by memory, before flying the airplane [[57:44|AC 90-109A App 7]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: plan a transition

body.p: **Build a training strategy before you fly.** AC 90-109A says to develop it with a CFI, preferably one with recent experience in the make and model [[57:5|AC 90-109A 5g]]. Best is your own airplane with that instructor, then the same make and model, then (for experimental airplanes) one with similar characteristics [[57:3|AC 90-109A 5f]].

bullets: 1. Rules: list the 61.31 training and endorsements the airplane needs [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(e)]] [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(f)]].
2. Hazards: identify them, assess severity and likelihood, mitigate, and consciously accept only the residual risk [[57:5|AC 90-109A 6a]] [[57:6|AC 90-109A 6a]].
3. Study: POH/AFM, supplements and the avionics pilot guide, system by system with the flow method [[57:14|AC 90-109A 8a]] [[57:15|AC 90-109A 8b]] [[30:53|RMH 7-4]].
4. Ground: cockpit familiarization and the blindfold test [[57:44|AC 90-109A App 7]]; avionics practice on a simulator or training device [[30:52|RMH 7-3]] [[30:53|RMH 7-4]].

5. Flight with the CFI: a structured syllabus [[24:248|AFH 12-17]]. Practice automation in VFR before IFR [[30:52|RMH 7-3]], and include manual flight after simulated automation failures [[15:13|AC 61-98E 2.2.3]].

6. After the endorsement: a conservative build-up, fewer people on board until familiar, and personal minimums [[57:6|AC 90-109A 6a]] [[57:7|AC 90-109A 6a]]. Raise your personal minimums for the unfamiliar airplane [[30:39|RMH 5-1]]. Type clubs recommend significant day VFR time before night or IFR [[57:4|AC 90-109A 5f]].
7. Keep it: a flight review in an automated aircraft should check automation competency and manual control [[15:26|AC 61-98E 4.3.3]] [[15:13|AC 61-98E 2.2.3]].

callout.text: The AFH syllabus times are only illustrations. Actual times depend on the pilot and may be shorter for highly qualified pilots or longer for those with little recent experience [[24:249|AFH 12-18]].

Instructors should simulate automation failures by safe means, for example disengaging an integrated autopilot on an approach, and should never actually make a system inoperative with switches or circuit breakers [[15:13|AC 61-98E 2.2.3]] [[15:14|AC 61-98E 2.2.3]].

check.q: In AC 90-109A, what are the three choices of airplane for transition training, best first?
check.a: The specific airplane you will fly, with a well-qualified instructor; then the same make and model; then, for experimental airplanes, one with similar characteristics [[57:3|AC 90-109A 5f]].

head: Error
Fix
rows: Flying with an expired chart or database because the app still opens
Verify currency yourself [[42:3|AC 91-78A 9.1]] [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17b1(c)(2)]]
Using a tablet moving map for IFR navigation
Under IFR it is only an aid to situational awareness [[33:101|AIM TBL 1-1-6]]
No plan for a dead tablet
Assess shutdown and failure before you need it [[42:4|AC 91-78A 11.1]]
Thinking 91.21 is only about passengers
Under IFR your own PED needs your determination too [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21]] [[42:2|AC 91-78A 7.2]]
Leaving the autopilot in a mode that no longer fits after a clearance change
Drop to basic modes, then reprogram [[30:51|RMH 7-2]]
Pushing a button and looking away
Anticipate, act, verify on the FMA [[30:51|RMH 7-2]] [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]
Treating the endorsement as the end of training
Build-up, fewer passengers, raised minimums [[57:6|AC 90-109A 6a]] [[57:7|AC 90-109A 6a]] [[30:39|RMH 5-1]]
Assuming a slower airplane is easy
Moving down carries as much risk as moving up [[57:3|AC 90-109A 5c]]

check.q: A friend with 3,000 hours in jets plans to rent a light, high-drag tailwheel airplane with no checkout. What two things do the sources say?
check.a: He needs tailwheel training and an endorsement to act as PIC [[60:215|14 CFR 61.31(i)]], and jet experience alone does not prepare a pilot for a low-inertia, high-drag airplane [[57:3|AC 90-109A 5c]].

f2.alt: A circle split into three colored segments with arrows running clockwise: Anticipate in orange at the top, Act in blue at the lower right, and Verify in green at the lower left, returning to Anticipate.

f3.alt: A black annunciator strip reading, left to right: LOC in white, HDG in green, AP in green, ALT in green, 9000FT in green, and GS in white.

f4.alt: A panel-mounted autopilot controller with a green display. Buttons along the top read ON, HDG, NAV, APR, REV, DN and along the bottom FD, YD, ATT, ALT, VS, UP. The screen shows HDG, APR ARM, VS HLD and VS400 with an up arrow.

Without a CFI, an experienced pilot willing to accompany leads to a familiarization flight; otherwise discuss to gain insight on characteristics.

Flight: training maneuvers, takeoffs, landings and go-arounds; emergency operations, control by reference to instruments, use of radio and autopilot; short and soft-field takeoffs and landings, maximum performance operations.

scenario.title: New glass, old habits
scenario.setup: You are instrument rated and fly a steam-gauge trainer twice a month. You just bought into a partnership on a fixed-gear, 310 hp single with flaps, a constant-speed prop, an electronic PFD and MFD and a two axis autopilot. You plan on a tablet with a Bluetooth ADS-B receiver. In six weeks you want to fly your spouse and two children 300 NM to a family event, in what is often IFR weather.

questions.q: What does Part 61 require before you act as PIC, and is there an endorsement for the glass panel?
questions.a: High-performance training and a one-time endorsement, since the engine is over 200 hp [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(f)]]; no complex endorsement, because the gear is fixed [[24:232|AFH 12-1]]. 61.31 has no glass-panel endorsement, but AC 61-98E recommends specialized TAA transition training with an instructor who knows the equipment [[15:26|AC 61-98E 4.3.3]].

questions.q: How should you pick your training?
questions.a: In your own airplane with a CFI who has recent experience in the make and model, the first choice in AC 90-109A [[57:3|AC 90-109A 5f]] [[57:5|AC 90-109A 5g]]. Use a structured syllabus [[24:248|AFH 12-17]].

questions.q: What will you study before the first lesson?
questions.a: Systems, procedures, performance and limitations, using the flow method [[57:14|AC 90-109A 8a]] [[57:15|AC 90-109A 8b]]; the avionics pilot guide and AFM supplements, with simulator practice [[30:53|RMH 7-4]] [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]]; and the cockpit layout until you pass a blindfold test [[57:44|AC 90-109A App 7]].

questions.q: On the IFR trip, may you use the tablet and its Bluetooth receiver?
questions.a: Yes, if you as PIC determine they will not interfere with the navigation or communication systems [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21]]. The EFB must also meet the AC 91-78A 9.1 tests, including current data [[42:3|AC 91-78A 9.1]], and under IFR its GPS map is only an aid to situational awareness [[33:101|AIM TBL 1-1-6]].

questions.q: Is the family trip in six weeks a good first long flight?
questions.a: AC 90-109A suggests a conservative build-up and fewer people on board until you are familiar [[57:6|AC 90-109A 6a]] [[57:7|AC 90-109A 6a]], and type clubs recommend significant day VFR before night or IFR [[57:4|AC 90-109A 5f]]. Raise your personal minimums for this airplane [[30:39|RMH 5-1]]. Application: unless you have that time, fly it solo or with a CFI first, or wait for good weather.

questions.q: In IMC on the approach, you switch the CDI from GPS to LOC and the airplane rolls wings level and starts drifting. What happened, and what do you do?
questions.a: Changing the navigation source dropped the autopilot NAV mode, and it defaulted to ROL [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]] [[30:52|RMH 7-3]]. Fly the airplane, reduce automation or hand fly if needed, reengage the mode, and verify on the FMA that it armed and engaged [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

skills.do: Given a new aircraft or avionics system, write and explain a transition plan: the 61.31 training and endorsements required, the hazards and mitigations, what to study (systems, procedures, performance, limitations, the avionics guide), ground and flight training with a qualified CFI including manual flight after automation failure, and the post-checkout limits (build-up, fewer passengers, raised personal minimums). Then say how you will use your EFB and other devices on that airplane within AC 91-78A and 91.21.
skills.practice: Pick the next airplane or avionics you might fly. Fill in the AC 90-109A 8a list [[57:14|AC 90-109A 8a]], trace two systems with the flow method [[57:15|AC 90-109A 8b]], and walk Figure 1 to choose your training [[57:4|AC 90-109A Fig 1]]. Use the AFH sample syllabus as a starting outline [[24:249|AFH 12-18]]. At your next flight review in an automated airplane, ask the instructor to evaluate automation competency and simulated automation failures [[15:26|AC 61-98E 4.3.3]] [[15:13|AC 61-98E 2.2.3]].

quiz.q: Under AC 91-78A, which of these may an EFB NOT replace?
options: Paper approach charts
A paper copy of the POH
A navigation receiver required by Part 91
A paper weight and balance worksheet
quiz.why: An EFB must not replace any system or equipment required by Part 91, such as a navigation, communication or surveillance system [[42:3|AC 91-78A 9.1]]. Charts, the POH and W&B are things it may show or compute [[42:2|AC 91-78A 8]].

quiz.q: Under AC 91-78A, how may a portable EFB use aircraft power?
options: It may never use aircraft power
Through a certificated power source, without depending on it to display
Only from a dedicated avionics bus
Only on the ground
quiz.why: A portable EFB is not dependent on a dedicated aircraft power source, although it may connect to aircraft power through a certificated power source [[42:3|AC 91-78A 10.1]].

quiz.q: Who decides on in-flight use of an EFB in place of paper under AC 91-78A?
options: The FAA, by letter of authorization
The app maker
The aircraft operator and the PIC
The aircraft mechanic who installed the mount
quiz.why: It is the decision of the aircraft operator and the PIC, with no formal operational approval if the AC is followed [[42:3|AC 91-78A 9.2]].

quiz.q: Which aircraft does AC 91.21-1D consider PED tolerant for the PEDs used with an installed system?
options: Any aircraft with a 28 volt electrical system
Aircraft with an FAA-approved system such as installed Wi-Fi
Any aircraft with a glass panel
Any aircraft flown only VFR
quiz.why: Aircraft with an FAA-approved system such as an onboard mobile telecommunications system, Wi-Fi, airborne access system or network control unit are considered PED tolerant for PEDs used with that system [[43:4|AC 91.21-1D 7.2.1]].

quiz.q: What low-power limit does AC 91.21-1D quote from RTCA DO-363?
options: 10 mW EIRP
100 mW EIRP
1 W EIRP
2.7 watt-hours
quiz.why: The quoted low-power limit is 100 mW EIRP, which includes Bluetooth [[43:8|AC 91.21-1D 10.3.2]]. 2.7 watt-hours is the AC's recommended limit per lithium ion cell, a different item [[43:8|AC 91.21-1D 10.5]].

quiz.q: In the RMH steps for interacting with automation, what does "anticipate" mean?
options: Engage the autopilot early so it is ready
Understand the system well enough to know what should happen before you push a button or turn a knob
Watch the FMA after the input
Ask ATC for the next clearance before you need it
quiz.why: Anticipate: understand the system well enough to know what should happen before pushing a button or turning a knob. Act is the input; verify is checking the result [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

quiz.q: According to the AIH, what does highly reliable automation tend to cause?
options: Faster scan rates
Overconfidence and complacency
Better crosschecking
Less need for checklists
quiz.why: Highly reliable automation has been shown to induce overconfidence and complacency, so the pilot may stop crosschecking [[25:18|AIH 1-14]].

quiz.q: The PHAK names a second critical information management skill for pilots new to advanced avionics. What is it?
options: Memorize every button sequence
Stop, look, and read
Always use the same keystrokes
Leave the default display settings
quiz.why: The second skill is stop, look, and read; reading before pushing, pulling or twisting can save trouble. Memorizing sequences is the trap it warns about [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]].

quiz.q: An experienced jet pilot plans to fly a light, high-drag airplane. What does AC 90-109A say?
options: Jet experience covers it
There is as much risk moving down in performance as moving up, so specific training is needed
Only a flight review is needed
Low-performance airplanes need no transition
quiz.why: Accident data shows as much risk moving down as moving up; high-speed experience alone does not prepare a pilot for a low-inertia, high-drag airplane [[57:3|AC 90-109A 5c]].

final_quiz.q: Your panel GPS is inoperative. Your tablet has a current database and an RNAV approach for the destination. May you fly the RNAV approach in IMC using the tablet?
options: Yes, if the database is current
No. VFR and hand-held GPS units are not authorized for IFR navigation or instrument approaches; under IFR they are only a situational awareness aid
Yes, if ATC approves
Yes, if you are the PIC and determine it does not interfere
final_quiz.why: VFR and hand-held GPS systems are not authorized for IFR navigation, instrument approaches or as a primary instrument flight reference [[33:101|AIM TBL 1-1-6]]. A 91.21 determination only covers interference [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21]], and an EFB may not replace required navigation equipment [[42:3|AC 91-78A 9.1]].

final_quiz.q: Night departure with your tablet on a kneeboard. Which setup best matches the AFH and AC 91-78A?
options: Full brightness so the chart is easy to read
Brightness set so it does not seriously impair night vision, and a plan for where it goes during takeoff and landing
Screen off until cruise, with no backup
Red filter only; stowage does not matter
final_quiz.why: The AFH says set EFB brightness so it does not seriously impair night vision [[24:222|AFH 11-5]]. AC 91-78A lists display and lighting, stowage during takeoff and landing, and an unsecured EFB as items to assess [[42:4|AC 91-78A 11.1]].

final_quiz.q: You want to bolt a permanent tablet bracket to the yoke. What do the sources say?
options: No approval is needed for anything related to a hand-held device
The bracket is an aircraft modification governed by part 43, so consult your mechanic
Only the tablet needs FAA approval
Brackets are prohibited
final_quiz.why: A hand-held unit needs no approval, but a permanent mounting bracket does; installing a panel- or yoke-mounted holder is governed by part 43 [[33:101|AIM TBL 1-1-6]] [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17b1(c)(3)]].

final_quiz.q: IFR in cruise, your CDI starts wandering right after a passenger switches on a portable Wi-Fi hotspot. Best action?
options: Ignore it; Wi-Fi is low power
Have the hotspot turned off, watch the CDI, and note the conditions
Switch to the tablet for navigation
Climb to get better reception
final_quiz.why: If interference is experienced, isolate the device, record the conditions and turn it off [[43:5|AC 91.21-1D 7.2.3]]. Wi-Fi devices often exceed the 100 mW low-power level [[43:8|AC 91.21-1D 10.3.2]].

final_quiz.q: You fly every leg on the autopilot from 400 ft AGL to 200 ft above minimums. Your IPC is next month. What do the sources point to?
options: Nothing; the autopilot is a risk control
Hand fly regularly; eroded manual skills hurt your ability to spot problems and recover from loss of control
Only practice programming faster
Ask the instructor to pull the autopilot breaker in flight
final_quiz.why: AC 61-98E says eroded skills degrade the ability to recognize system issues and recover from LOC, and recommends manual control at times [[15:13|AC 61-98E 2.2.2]]. Instructors should not pull breakers to simulate failures [[15:14|AC 61-98E 2.2.3]].

final_quiz.q: Night VFR over mountains in a glass-panel airplane. Which display tactic does the PHAK suggest?
options: Show every weather layer at once
Use the MFD terrain awareness page and the nearest airports inset
Set the map to the widest scale and leave it
Turn the MFD off to save night vision
final_quiz.why: The PHAK lists using the terrain awareness page for night or IMC flight near mountains and the nearest airports inset at night or over inhospitable terrain [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]].

final_quiz.q: In a PHAK study, when given a late change to a parallel runway's approach, how did EFIS crews compare with analog crews?
options: They did better because the FMS did the work
They went head down a long time reprogramming; disengaging the automation and hand flying would have been easier
There was no difference
They declined the change
final_quiz.why: The EFIS crews had a harder time and went head down programming; the approach would have been easier by disengaging the automation and flying it manually [[1:66|PHAK 2-27]].

final_quiz.q: You got a complex endorsement in 2005 and have never flown anything over 180 hp. Can you act as PIC of a 285 hp fixed-gear airplane after a checkout with no endorsement?
options: Yes, the complex endorsement covers it
No, you need high-performance training and a one-time endorsement, unless you logged high-performance PIC time before August 4, 1997
Yes, if the airplane is a TAA
No, you need a type rating
final_quiz.why: More than 200 hp makes it high-performance, and a complex endorsement does not cover it. 61.31(f) requires training and a one-time endorsement; the exceptions are high-performance PIC time logged before August 4, 1997, or a 135.293 competency check in one [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(f)]] [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(f)]].

final_quiz.q: You are buying an amateur-built airplane whose builder put the fuel selector in an odd place. Which AC 90-109A step most directly targets that hazard?
options: A longer cross-country on the first flight
Sitting in the cockpit until you can find every control without searching, and flying first with a previous operator, instructor or the builder
Adding an AOA indicator
Reading internet forums
final_quiz.why: Appendix 7 recommends learning control positions on the ground (the blindfold test) and flying with a previous operator, instructor or the builder before solo [[57:44|AC 90-109A App 7]] [[57:45|AC 90-109A App 7]].

final_quiz.q: An airline first officer rents a light piston single for a weekend trip. Which AC 90-109A point is most relevant?
options: Airline training satisfies all transition needs
Moving to a slower, single-pilot airplane brings its own challenges: weather and headwinds hit harder and avionics may be less capable
Only the 61.31 endorsements matter
Light singles need no checklist
final_quiz.why: AC 90-109A Appendix 10 lists the challenges of moving down in performance and notes that going from multi-crew to single pilot creates its own challenges [[57:52|AC 90-109A App 10]].

final_quiz.q: Your alternator fails. When is this most likely an emergency rather than an inconvenience, per AC 90-109A?
options: Day VFR in the local area
At night or in IFR
Only on the ground
Only in a high-performance airplane
final_quiz.why: AC 90-109A notes an alternator failure is likely an inconvenience in day VFR local flying but could be an emergency at night or in IFR [[57:18|AC 90-109A 8c]].

final_quiz.q: Which item is part of the 14 CFR 61.129(j) description of a TAA?
options: A three-axis autopilot with autothrottle
A two axis autopilot integrated with the navigation and heading guidance system
Synthetic vision
An installed EFB
final_quiz.why: A TAA needs an electronic PFD, an MFD with a GPS moving map, and a two axis autopilot integrated with the navigation and heading guidance system, with the PFD and MFD elements continuously visible [[60:321|14 CFR 61.129(j)]].

final_quiz.q: Your ADS-B In display shows no traffic ahead in the pattern. What does the AIM say?
options: You can rely on it; every aircraft must be shown
It assists visual acquisition only and does not relieve you of see and avoid; not every aircraft will appear
Use it to plan avoidance maneuvers in IMC
It replaces the traffic advisory from the tower
final_quiz.why: The ADS-B traffic display is not a collision avoidance system and does not relieve see and avoid [[33:304|AIM 4-5-7e]]; in some airspace not all aircraft have ADS-B Out or transponders [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g]].

takeaways: An EFB may replace paper when it shows the same information, uses current data you have verified, replaces no required equipment, and meets 91.21.
Your tablet is a PED: under IFR, you as PIC must determine it will not interfere.
Suspect a device? Isolate it, note the conditions, turn it off.
A tablet moving map has no RAIM and no accuracy standard: under IFR it is only a situational awareness aid.
Anticipate, act, verify on every input, and drop to basic modes when the plan changes.
Hand fly regularly and actively monitor; automation bias and complacency are the hazards.
A transition is more than a 61.31 endorsement: study the systems, train with a CFI who knows the airplane, then build up slowly with raised minimums.
cfi_notes: AC 91.21-1D 8.3 still points to "AC 91-78, Use of Class 1 or Class 2 EFB" [[43:6|AC 91.21-1D 8.3]], which AC 91-78A canceled [[42:1|AC 91-78A 4]]. Teach the AC 91-78A portable and installed terms.
AC 91.21-1D paragraph 1 describes 91.21 as an IFR rule [[43:1|AC 91.21-1D 1]]; the rule also covers aircraft of certificate holders in any conditions [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21]]. Teach the CFR text.
The sources disagree on the year of the Colombia FMS accident: the RMH says 1995 [[30:52|RMH 7-3]] and the PHAK says 1999 [[1:71|PHAK 2-32]]. Teach the lesson, not the date.

The 100 mW Bluetooth quote sits in AC 91.21-1D's cargo-tracker section [[43:8|AC 91.21-1D 10.3.2]]. Treat it as background; under IFR the PIC determination in 91.21(b)(5) still applies [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21]].
Passenger devices, the PED briefing and M-PEDs are taught in RF.IV.D. Keep this lesson on the pilot's own devices and the aircraft.

There is no 61.31 endorsement for glass panels or autopilots. At a flight review, evaluate automation competency in the airplane the pilot normally flies [[15:26|AC 61-98E 4.3.3]], and simulate failures by disengaging the autopilot, never by pulling breakers [[15:13|AC 61-98E 2.2.3]] [[15:14|AC 61-98E 2.2.3]].
Many refresher pilots fly for airlines. Use AC 90-109A Appendix 10: moving from multi-crew to single pilot and to lower performance has its own risks [[57:52|AC 90-109A App 10]].
AC 90-109A is aimed at experimental airplanes, but it says its recommendations apply to unfamiliar type-certificated airplanes too [[57:2|AC 90-109A 3d]]. Figure 1 works for any transition.
The PHAK still frames manual skill as flying to "the PTS" [[1:68|PHAK 2-29]]. Application: hold the pilot to the standards for the certificate they hold.
gaps: AC 120-76 (which defines Type A and Type B EFB applications) and AC 20-173 (EFB installation) are not in the sources.
No source gives tablet battery, heat, mounting-strength or backup-device rules; use the device maker's guidance and your own failure plan.
RTCA DO-307A and DO-363, InFO 13010 and 47 CFR 22.925 are cited but not in the sources, and no source gives a step-by-step way to test one device for interference in a light airplane.
Autopilot mode logic, mode colors and reversion behavior differ by system; the AFM supplement and pilot guide, not these sources, give them.
The GAMA Transition Training Master Syllabus, type club programs and insurance checkout requirements are not in the sources.

activities.title: True or false: EFBs
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: AC 91-78A is mandatory for Part 91 pilots who use an EFB.
cards.why: False. It is not mandatory and is not a regulation, but if you use its means you follow it in all important respects [[42:1|AC 91-78A 1]].

cards.s: In-flight use of a Type A or Type B EFB application in place of paper needs no formal operational approval if the AC is followed.
There is no regulatory requirement to update a GPS database for VFR navigation.
cards.why: True, though it is recommended and an outdated map should not be used near critical airspace [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17b1(c)(2)]].

cards.s: Hand-held GPS units have RAIM alerting, so they warn you of a bad position.
cards.why: False. VFR panel-mount and hand-held units have no RAIM alerting [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17b1(c)(1)]].

cards.s: The PHAK says to assume data link weather is at least 7 to 8 minutes older than its time stamp.
AC 91-78A says EFB training should include procedures for cross-checking data entry and computed information.

activities.title: Who decides under 91.21?
activities.intro: All flights are in a privately owned or flying club airplane (no certificate holder). Tap each item, then tap where it belongs.
buckets: Allowed only if the PIC or operator determines no interference
Not limited by 91.21 on this flight

items.t: A hearing aid on an IFR flight
A portable voice recorder on an IFR flight
An electric shaver on an IFR flight
Your tablet EFB on an IFR flight
A Bluetooth ADS-B receiver on an IFR flight
A passenger laptop on an IFR flight
Your tablet EFB on a VFR flight
A passenger camera on a VFR sightseeing flight

activities.why: 91.21(a) applies to certificate holders' aircraft and other aircraft under IFR; (b) excepts the named devices and those the operator has determined will not interfere; (c) lets the PIC or other operator decide on non-certificate-holder aircraft [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21]].

activities.title: Read the mode annunciator
activities.intro: Drag each label to the annunciator it describes.

pins.label: Lateral mode now steering the airplane
Vertical mode now holding the airplane

activities.title: Work the numbers: how old is the picture?
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Two airplanes are head-on, each at 120 knots. TIS-B can take up to 13 seconds between updates. How far do they close in 13 seconds?
items.why: Closure 120 + 120 = 240 knots. 240 x 13 / 3600 = 0.87 NM. TIS-B updates every 3 to 13 seconds [[33:306|AIM 4-5-8d2(c)]].

items.q: The same two airplanes, but with ADS-B updating about once per second. How far do they close between updates, in feet? (1 NM = 6,076 ft)
items.why: 240 x 1 / 3600 = 0.0667 NM. 0.0667 x 6,076 = 405 ft. ADS-B updates nominally once per second [[33:306|AIM 4-5-8d2(c)]].

items.q: Your data link radar image is time-stamped 6 minutes ago. Using the PHAK's 8 minutes of extra age, how far has a cell moving at 30 knots traveled since the data was collected?
items.why: Age = 6 + 8 = 14 minutes. 30 x 14 / 60 = 7.0 NM. The PHAK says to assume data link weather is at least 7 to 8 minutes older than shown [[1:334|PHAK 13-24]].

items.q: AC 90-109A says headwinds hurt slower airplanes more, as a percentage. A 25 knot headwind cuts what percent off the groundspeed of a 95 knot airplane?
For the 95 knot airplane on a 150 NM leg, how many extra minutes does that 25 knot headwind add compared with no wind?
items.why: No wind: 150 / 95 x 60 = 94.7 min. Headwind: groundspeed 95 - 25 = 70 knots, 150 / 70 x 60 = 128.6 min. Difference 33.9, about 34 min [[57:52|AC 90-109A App 10]].

activities.title: Which document?
activities.intro: Tap a source, then what it covers.

pairs.r: Replacing paper with an EFB under Part 91
Deciding which PEDs may be used aboard
Training and endorsement for complex airplanes
Training and endorsement for engines over 200 hp
Becoming familiar with all available information before flight

activities.title: Build the transition
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put these in order, then tap Check.
steps: List the 61.31 training and endorsements the airplane needs
Study the POH/AFM, supplements and avionics pilot guide system by system
Learn the cockpit on the ground until you pass a blindfold test
Ground and flight training with a CFI experienced in the make and model
Fly solo day VFR with raised personal minimums and a slow build-up
Add passengers, night and IFR after significant day VFR time
activities.why: Rules first [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(f)]]; study [[57:14|AC 90-109A 8a]]; know the cockpit before flying it [[57:44|AC 90-109A App 7]]; train with a qualified CFI [[57:5|AC 90-109A 5g]], who endorses you [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(e)]]; build up and limit people on board until familiar [[57:6|AC 90-109A 6a]] [[57:7|AC 90-109A 6a]] [[30:39|RMH 5-1]]; significant day VFR before night or IFR [[57:4|AC 90-109A 5f]].

activities.title: First real trip in the new airplane
activities.intro: You finished your transition training in a glass-panel single last week. Today you fly IFR alone to an airport 150 NM away, with your tablet as EFB.

steps.s: After engine start, one engine indication on the MFD still shows a red X. What do you do?
options: Take off; it will clear in flight
Follow the AFM/POH check and do not depart until the system check passes
Use the tablet's engine page instead
Pull and reset breakers until it clears
steps.why: Glass-panel ground checks include system-driven removal of X's over engine indicators, done as the AFM/POH specifies [[24:42|AFH 2-5]]; EFIS checks verify no red X's are displayed [[24:345|AFH 17-11]].

steps.s: In the climb, your tablet shuts down and will not restart. What now?
options: Return at once; you cannot fly IFR without the tablet
Fly the airplane, then continue on the installed avionics and your planned backup
Hand the airplane to the autopilot and troubleshoot head down until it works
Descend VFR below the clouds
steps.why: The EFB may not replace required equipment [[42:3|AC 91-78A 9.1]], and its shutdown and failure should already be assessed [[42:4|AC 91-78A 11.1]]. Application: that is why you planned a backup.

steps.s: In cruise, the GPS position on the MFD jumps about 2 NM and disagrees with the VOR. What do you do?
options: Trust GPS; VORs are older
Cross-check with conventional navaids, tell ATC about the GPS problem, and be ready to navigate without GPS
Reset the GPS and keep going direct
Switch to the tablet's GPS
steps.why: Verify position with conventional navaids [[33:119|AIM 1-2-4f]], promptly tell ATC about GPS degradation, and be prepared to operate without GPS [[33:118|AIM 1-2-4a]].

steps.s: Near the destination, ATC changes your approach at short notice. Workload is high and you are in IMC. What is the best first move?
options: Leave the autopilot in NAV and reprogram the whole approach head down
Select heading and altitude on the autopilot, comply with ATC, then load and check the new approach
Disconnect everything and reprogram while hand flying
Refuse the change
steps.why: Move to a lower level of automation that keeps the flight path under control while you reprogram [[30:51|RMH 7-2]]. Then verify the new procedure is what you expect [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]].

steps.s: Established on the new approach, the FMA shows the lateral mode armed in white, and it stays white as you cross the final course. What do you do?
options: Wait; it will capture eventually
Fly the airplane on course (heading mode or by hand), then find out why the mode did not engage
Descend to minimums anyway
Turn the autopilot off and on until it captures
steps.why: Verify that armed functions engage at the right time [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]. If the automation is not doing what you expect, reduce the level or fly manually and take time to resolve it [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].
